hero.title: Landing page or website: what do you actually need?
hero.intro: The two terms are often used interchangeably, even though they serve different purposes. The difference isn't scope — it's goal.

keyTakeaway.title: In short
keyTakeaway.text: A website represents your entire business and is built to last. A landing page pursues a single, often time-limited goal — a campaign or an offer. Both have their place, but rarely the same one.

sections.heading: What a website is meant to do
paragraphs: A website is the complete digital representation of your business: who you are, what you offer, how to reach you, what references exist. It's built to last over a long period and to serve several different visitor interests at once.

That breadth is both its strength and its limit: a website can answer many different questions, but it can't deliver one perfectly tailored message for every single ad campaign without becoming cluttered.

sections.heading: What a landing page is meant to do
paragraphs: A landing page pursues exactly one goal — a signup, an enquiry, an offer. It's deliberately built without distraction: no extensive menu, no ten equally-weighted options, just a clear path to a single action. It's typically tied to a specific campaign, a time-limited offer, or a product launch.

That focus isn't a downside — it's the whole point: someone arriving from an ad should see exactly the message that matches the ad, instead of having to navigate a general website to find the offer they were looking for.

sections.heading: Typical use cases for a website
paragraphs: You run an established business with several services. Customers should be able to inform themselves, compare, and decide which area is relevant to them. You need a structure that holds up over months and years and can grow with the business.

sections.heading: Typical use cases for a landing page
paragraphs: You're running ads for a specific offer and want visitors to land directly on the matching message. You're launching something new and still small, and need a fast, first digital presence. You're testing an offer for a limited time and don't want to build a permanent structure around it.

sections.heading: What if both apply?
paragraphs: Often the right answer isn't "either-or": an established business can have a full website as its foundation and use dedicated landing pages for individual campaigns on top of it. The website remains the permanent base; the landing page handles the short-term, focused task.

In practice, this combination works particularly well for seasonal offers, product launches, or time-limited marketing campaigns: the main website stays unchanged while one or more landing pages exist in parallel for the specific campaign.

sections.heading: How to tell which one you need right now
paragraphs: A simple guiding question helps: should this page represent your business as a whole, or should it trigger exactly one action? In the first case, a website is the right choice; in the second, a landing page. If you're unsure, it helps to look at your concrete goal for the coming weeks rather than trying to make one permanent decision for all time.
